objectives: Link Jira issues and Confluence pages in both directions
Embed live Jira tables in Confluence using JQL
Create Jira issues directly from Confluence requirement text
Use Jira and Confluence together for traceability and release notes

terminology.definition: A Confluence element that embeds one Jira issue or a live table of issues from a JQL query.
A pasted URL that Confluence renders as a rich preview showing key details such as issue status.
A Jira field identifying the release in which an issue is delivered.
A summary of what changed in a release, often generated from Jira issues.
Keeping each piece of information in one authoritative place and linking to it elsewhere.
Settings that control who can view or edit spaces, pages and projects.

exercises.question: Write the JQL you'd use in a Confluence macro to show all stories and bugs in epic SHOP-5 that are not Done.
exercises.answer: `parent = SHOP-5 AND type in (Story, Bug) AND status != Done ORDER BY rank` *(older Jira versions may use "Epic Link" = SHOP-5)*.

exercises.question: Describe a workflow that takes a requirement from a Confluence page into a Jira story and back.
exercises.answer: Highlight the requirement text on the approved page and create a Jira issue from it, so the issue and page link automatically. Refine the story in Jira with AC and an estimate. Back on the page, embed a Jira issues macro filtered on the epic so the story's status shows live.

exercises.question: Why is copying story text from Jira into Confluence a bad idea?
exercises.answer: The two copies drift apart when either changes, so readers can't tell which is correct. Linking or embedding live issues keeps one source of truth and always shows current status.

quiz.question: The best way to show live story status on a Confluence page is:
options: Embed a Jira issues macro with a JQL filter
quiz.explanation: The macro updates automatically from Jira.

quiz.question: Which Jira field is used to generate release notes?
quiz.explanation: fixVersion identifies the release an issue is delivered in.

quiz.question: Stakeholders see 'restricted' instead of Jira issues on a page. The most likely cause is:
options: They lack permission to view the Jira project
quiz.explanation: Viewers need Jira permissions to see embedded issues.

quiz.question: Creating a Jira issue from highlighted Confluence text:
options: Creates an issue that links back to the page
quiz.explanation: The issue and page are linked automatically, supporting traceability.

quiz.question: Which belongs in Confluence rather than Jira?
options: Detailed business rules shared by several stories
quiz.explanation: Shared rules and context belong in one Confluence page linked from stories.

interview.question: How do you use Jira and Confluence together?
interview.answer: Confluence holds the context (requirements pages per epic, business rules, process maps, decisions, meeting notes) and Jira holds the work items. I create stories from requirement text so they link automatically, embed live Jira tables on requirement pages, link decisions from stories, and generate release notes from fixVersion. That gives lightweight end-to-end traceability.

interview.question: How would you give stakeholders visibility of progress without status meetings?
interview.answer: Add live Jira macros and an epic progress or roadmap view to the Confluence epic pages, share a dashboard, make sure permissions allow access, and add a short written summary each sprint. Then use the Sprint Review for discussion rather than status reporting.

interview.question: How would you provide audit-ready traceability using Atlassian tools?
interview.answer: Approved requirements pages with version history; Jira stories created from and linked to those requirements; test cases in Xray or Zephyr linked to stories with execution results; fixVersions for releases; decision records linked to affected stories; and a Confluence report page pulling these together with JQL macros.

assignment.title: Connect your tools
assignment.brief:
Using your practice Jira project and Confluence space (or documents simulating them):
1. Create two stories from requirement text on your epic page.
2. Embed a live list of the epic's stories on the page.
3. Link a decision record from a story.
4. Create a release notes page for a fixVersion with a human summary at the top.
deliverables: Screenshots or description of linked page and stories
